q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE difference between the Soviet and Chinese communist revolutions.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the Sino-Soviet split, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Sino-Soviet split affected the Cold War.

sample_answers.a: The Russian Revolution was led by urban workers and soldiers in the capital cities, while the Chinese Revolution was based on the peasantry, with Mao's Red Army building rural base areas during the Long March before taking the cities.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, Mao rejected Khrushchev's de-Stalinization and peaceful coexistence as betrayals of revolution, while Khrushchev saw Mao's radicalism as dangerous; their incompatible claims to lead world communism made the alliance unsustainable.
sample_answers.c: The split allowed the United States to play China against the Soviet Union, culminating in Nixon's 1972 visit to Beijing; the communist bloc was no longer monolithic, which reduced Soviet power and reshaped Cold War diplomacy.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the Sino-Soviet split — the bitter rupture between the world's two great communist powers — as the result of both ideological differences and national rivalries. The Russian and Chinese revolutions had followed different paths: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in cities through a disciplined vanguard party, while Mao's Communists built a peasant-based army in the countryside over decades of guerrilla war. These different experiences produced different doctrines. When Khrushchev denounced Stalin and preached 'peaceful coexistence' with capitalism, Mao accused him of revisionism — of betraying the revolution. Beneath the ideological quarrel lay older tensions: border disputes, Soviet condescension toward China, and Mao's determination that China would never again submit to foreign domination, even by a socialist ally.
—Historian's account of Soviet and Chinese communism in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE criticism Khrushchev makes of Stalin's rule.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Khrushchev's speech signaled a change in Soviet policy.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Mao Zedong reacted negatively to Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin.

sample_answers.a: Khrushchev accuses Stalin of establishing a 'cult of personality,' using terror against loyal party members, and distorting socialist legality through purges and forced confessions.
sample_answers.b: By publicly condemning Stalin's crimes, Khrushchev signaled that the Soviet Union would move away from mass terror toward 'peaceful coexistence' with the West and a less violent form of communist rule.
sample_answers.c: Mao had modeled his own leadership on Stalin's and feared that de-Stalinization would undermine his authority; he also saw Khrushchev's attack on Stalin as the first step toward abandoning revolution altogether.

q2.stimulus:
Stalin acted not through persuasion, explanation, and patient cooperation with people, but by imposing his concepts and demanding absolute submission to his opinion. Whoever opposed this concept or tried to prove his viewpoint met with expulsion from the leadership, followed by moral and physical annihilation. The cult of the individual acquired such monstrous size chiefly because Stalin himself encouraged and supported the glorification of his own person. We must abolish the cult of the individual decisively, once and for all.
—Adapted from Nikita Khrushchev's 'secret speech' denouncing Stalin, delivered to the Soviet Communist Party Congress, 1956

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map regarding communist influence in Eurasia.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why communism spread widely in Eurasia but not in Western Europe after 1945.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the map reflects a change in the communist world between 1950 and 1970.

sample_answers.a: Communist parties or states controlled a vast continuous bloc stretching from Eastern Europe through the Soviet Union to China, covering much of the Eurasian landmass by the mid-twentieth century.
sample_answers.b: In Eastern Europe and China, communists came to power through war, occupation, or revolution against collapsed old orders, while in Western Europe, American aid, democratic institutions, and stronger economies contained communist appeal.
sample_answers.c: The map shows both the Soviet Union and China as major communist powers, but by the 1960s they had split into hostile rivals; the apparently unified communist bloc visible on the map masked a deep and growing Sino-Soviet division.

q3.stimulus: The map shows the extent of communist influence in Eurasia, with communist states and regions where communist parties held power marked across Eastern Europe, the Soviet Union, Mongolia, China, and parts of Southeast Asia. The map illustrates how, by the mid-twentieth century, communist governments controlled a large portion of the world's most populous continent.
